case_studies.title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
case_studies.abstract: Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that a hybrid AI stack—using local open‑source models for routine tasks and commercial services for complex work—can cut commercial AI costs by up to 36% for a small tech firm. They built a system that offloads 90% of coordination and documentation work to self‑hosted models while still relying on commercial agents for heavy inference. This demonstrates a practical way to reduce spending without sacrificing functionality.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, first map your team’s routine AI tasks (e.g., documentation, context‑transfer) to local models; second, set up a central deployment that routes these to self‑hosted services; third, monitor cost savings and user adoption, adjusting the split between local and commercial models as needed.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses a hybrid self-hosted AI stack that reduces commercial AI costs by moving lower-complexity tasks to local models. This is directly relevant to infrastructure engineers managing AI workloads and SaaS tools, providing a concrete deployment approach with real cost savings. The experience is based on actual deployment at a software company, indicating a usable system rather than pure theory, but it lacks publicly released code or a reusable framework, limiting immediate reuse. The approach can be adopted by other IT teams within a short timeframe to cut inference costs and improve control, offering tangible monetisation potential. The scores reflect moderate to high real-world relevance, medium maturity, and moderate immediate applicability.

case_studies.title: SKIM: Pruning Large Language Model Agents via Selective Knowledge Informed Masking
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed under structured generation, where grammar constraints enforce output format at inference time. Whereas existing compression methods target unconstrained generation, we first identify a fundamental mismatch: under structured generation, grammar constraints reduce the model's output distribution to valid tokens, and the logits matter most at the small set of positions that decide the agent's action. Motivated by this finding, we propose SKIM (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking), the first pruning and distillation framework for LLM agents under structured generation, with both stages guided by token role. SKIM partitions token positions into context, decision, and format categories, and this partition drives two complementary axes: (1) category-aware pruning saliency scores that preserve parameters most relevant for decision positions; and (2) an on-policy distillation objective that aligns student and teacher on valid tokens, paired with category-aware feature matching. We evaluate SKIM on tool-calling benchmarks and within multi-step agent loops, across multiple model scales and sparsity levels. SKIM consistently improves accuracy over baselines, with its superiority becoming most striking in high-sparsity regimes where conventional methods struggle, demonstrating the potential of category-aware compression for deployment-time grammar-constrained agents.
case_studies.summary: SKIM tackles the challenge of making large language model agents more efficient when they must follow strict grammar rules, such as in tool‑calling workflows. The authors built a pruning and distillation method that focuses on the few token positions that decide actions, keeping the most important parameters and matching the model’s behaviour on valid outputs. In tests, SKIM kept accuracy high even when models were heavily compressed, outperforming standard pruning techniques.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud infrastructure for LLM services, here is what to do:
1. Identify the token positions in your agent that are ‘decision’ points (where the model chooses actions). 2. Apply a category‑aware pruning tool that keeps parameters tied to those decision positions. 3. Use on‑policy distillation to fine‑tune the pruned model against the original on valid token sets before deploying.
case_studies.score_reasoning: SKIM targets LLM agents used in structured generation, which aligns with the IT engineer’s use of LLM APIs, agentic systems, and deployment optimizations. The paper presents a concrete pruning/distillation framework with empirical results on tool‑calling benchmarks, indicating a working system rather than a pure theory. The method could be incorporated into existing LLM deployment pipelines or sold as a performance‑improvement service for SaaS or cloud‑based LLM offerings. However, it is specialized to grammar‑constrained agents and not a general infrastructure solution, so scores are moderate. The paper has a clear implementation path but would require integration effort, hence the moderate maturity and monetisation scores.

case_studies.title: Decision Models as Retrieval Gates Against Injection and Pollution
case_studies.abstract: Retrieved web text can carry instructions aimed at the language model, or synthetic pages written to mislead. We test whether released open-weight decision models, which answer typed questions about a text without generating tokens, can screen retrieved passages against both threats. On a benchmark of 1,000 questions over forum-style web pages with hidden injected instructions, a Kev-4B gate reads each passage's HTML. Attack success, measured automatically, falls from 27.9% with no defence to 13.6% with the published mitigations (sanitisation, normalisation and citation prompting) and to 5.7% with the gate added. The gate takes 76 ms per passage and wrongly flags 4 of 186 benign pages with instructions for human readers. Responsiveness on clean queries stays within a point (85.6% to 86.2%). On a 200-query pollution testbed where two thirds of the candidate pages are fake, filtering the pool before the top ten are chosen keeps fake pages out of the answer (0.5% exposure) and holds accuracy at 83%, against 28% with no filter. Filtering only the top ten leaves the generator too few pages to answer. Large LLMs used as judges rank attacks better (AUROC 0.99 against 0.94) but cost ten times more. Gates catch more attacks when they read the page's HTML than when they read its plain text. Every model is open-weight.
case_studies.summary: This research shows that a lightweight decision model can act as a filter to stop malicious or misleading content from tricking language models. They built a Kev-4B gate that scans HTML and cuts injection success from 27.9% to 5.7%, with only 76 ms per page and a small false‑positive rate. The result is a cheaper, faster defence that keeps most queries safe while keeping performance nearly unchanged.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑based LLM services, add a gate like Kev‑4B to your retrieval pipeline: step 1, run the gate on each retrieved page; step 2, discard pages flagged as potential injection or pollution; step 3, pass only clean pages to the generation model. This reduces injection risk from ~28% to ~6% and keeps accuracy high. The gate costs only 76 ms per page and is open‑weight, making it easy to integrate.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical gate that can be integrated into existing LLM retrieval pipelines to reduce injection and pollution attacks, directly affecting IT engineers working on secure LLM deployments. The method is experimentally validated with open-weight models and offers a usable, low-latency solution, but it is still at the research prototype stage with no commercial release. The monetisation potential is modest, as engineers could adopt it as a security layer, but it would require custom integration and is not a ready‑to‑sell service.

case_studies.title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
case_studies.abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.
case_studies.summary: Meta access lets an AI assistant see and interact with the whole workspace of a chat client, not just the conversation. The authors built a prototype that provides structured, permissioned access to interface elements, settings, and context, enabling the AI to organise and operate the UI. The result is a single entry point that turns chat into a control layer for the whole workspace, with risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection and trust.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1. Ensure your cloud‑hosted chat or agentic tools expose a structured API for interface state and permissions. 2. Implement a control‑plane boundary so the AI cannot alter your settings without confirmation. 3. Monitor for prompt‑injection or unauthorized changes in the workspace to mitigate trust risks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses meta access to software UIs via LLMs, which could influence how engineers interact with tools and potentially improve automation and control layers. However, the work appears to be at a prototype stage with limited published code or real deployment, indicating low maturity. While there is some conceptual commercial potential (e.g., building UI‑control layers or accessibility enhancements), it is not yet actionable within 90 days. Thus moderate impact, low maturity, and modest monetisation potential lead to a total of 30.
